content: Torticollis, also known as wry neck or loxia, is a condition characterized by an abnormal twisting of the neck. In this condition, the head tilts to one side while the chin rotates to the opposite side. Symptoms of Torticollis: The range of motion of the head is limited. Patients may experience headaches. Head tremors can occur. Neck pain is a common symptom. One shoulder may appear higher than the other. The neck muscles may feel stiff. Swelling of the neck muscles may be present, and in some cases, this swelling is noticeable at birth. Causes of Torticollis: Torticollis can be inherited, resulting from specific genetic changes. It can also be acquired, developing due to damage to the nervous system or muscles. If the condition arises without a known cause, it is referred to as idiopathic torticollis. Torticollis can develop during childhood or adulthood. Congenital torticollis, present at birth, may occur if the fetus's head is positioned incorrectly in the womb or if the neck muscles or blood supply to the neck are injured. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Contact a healthcare provider if symptoms do not improve with treatment or if new symptoms develop. Torticollis that occurs after an injury or in association with an illness may indicate a serious condition. Immediate medical attention is necessary in such cases. Diagnosis: A physical examination often reveals visible shortening of the neck muscles. The head tilts toward the affected side, while the chin points to the opposite side. In severe cases, the entire head may be pulled and turned to one side. An electromyogram (EMG) may be performed in mild cases to identify which muscles are most affected. Treatment Options: For congenital torticollis, treatment involves stretching the shortened neck muscles. Passive stretching and positioning are commonly used in infants and young children, with a high success rate if initiated within the first three months of life. If other treatments fail, surgery to correct the neck muscle may be performed during the preschool years. Acquired torticollis is treated by addressing the underlying cause. Heat application, cervical spine traction, and massage may help alleviate head and neck pain. Stretching exercises and neck braces can assist in managing muscle spasms. Medications such as the anticholinergic drug baclofen may be prescribed. Botulinum toxin injections can provide temporary relief, but repeated injections every three months are typically required. Surgery is rarely used. Prognosis: The condition is often easier to correct in infants and children. However, if it becomes chronic, nerve root compression in the neck may lead to numbness and tingling. The affected muscle may also become hypertrophic (enlarged) due to constant stimulation and use. Botulinum toxin injections frequently offer significant relief. Possible Complications: Muscle swelling may occur due to constant tension. Neurological symptoms, such as those caused by compressed nerve roots, may develop. Prevention: While there is no known way to prevent torticollis, early treatment can help prevent the condition from worsening.
